tax.title: The billionaire tax and its two challengers
tax.summary: Prop 40 creates a one-time wealth tax. Props 41 and 42 are general tax rules, but each is written to apply to taxes on this same ballot, and each conflicts with a feature of Prop 40. The LAO prints the same warning on all three measures: if Prop 41 or 42 gets more yes votes than Prop 40, Prop 40 could be stopped even if a majority approves it.
tax.body:
Each challenger hits a different feature of Prop 40:

  • Prop 41 bars any new tax from being excluded from the [[gann|state spending limit]]. Prop 40 excludes its revenue from that limit.
  • Prop 42 bars new taxes on owning [[personal-property|personal property]] and taxes based on past residency. Prop 40 taxes net worth and uses residency on January 1, 2026.

Under the [[conflict|conflicting measures rule]], the margin matters as much as passage. A voter who supports Prop 40 and also votes yes on 41 or 42 may be adding votes that could cancel it.

Props 41 and 42 also have lasting effects beyond Prop 40: audits of every future special tax (41), and a permanent constitutional bar on wealth-style taxes (42).

Prop 40Props 41 / 42Likely result for the billionaire tax
FailsAny resultNo tax.
PassesBoth failTax takes effect (subject to any other legal challenge).
Passes41 or 42 passes, with fewer yes votes than 40Prop 40 generally prevails where they conflict, so the tax likely takes effect. 41 and 42 still apply to future taxes.
Passes41 or 42 passes, with more yes votes than 40Courts could find a conflict and stop Prop 40.

Source: LAO analyses of Props 40, 41, and 42, Official Voter Information Guide. Courts decide whether measures conflict; the table describes the general rule, not a guaranteed outcome.

Money context: Building a Better California, whose top donors the FPPC lists as Sergey Brin and John Doerr, has put about $245 million into No on 40, Yes on 41, and Yes on 42 combined. SEIU-UHW has put about $32 million into Yes on 40.

budget.title: State budget: borrowing, saving, and taxing
budget.summary: These measures don't conflict legally, but together they shape the state budget for decades. Two add long-term debt, one changes savings rules, one keeps an existing tax, and one uses a different kind of borrowing that doesn't touch the General Fund.
budget.body:
PropEffect on the state budgetTiming
1$500–600M a year to repay $11.25B in [[go-bond|general obligation bonds]]~25 years
38$500–600M a year to repay $8.4B in bonds, possibly offset by research revenue~20 years
2More money held in reserve; extra debt payments extended to 2040Ongoing
3Keeps $5–15B a year in income tax revenueFrom 2031
37No direct state cost: $25B in [[revenue-bond|revenue bonds]] repaid by borrowersOngoing

Props 1 and 38 together would cost about $1 billion a year from the General Fund for roughly two decades. For scale, Prop 3's revenue, if approved, would be about 5–15 times that. Prop 2 changes how much of good-year revenue must be saved before it can be spent.

housing.title: Housing cost and supply
housing.summary: Three different approaches to housing. They don't conflict and could all pass.
housing.body:
PropApproachWho it mainly helpsWho pays
1Public money for affordable rental construction, homeownership help, veterans' loansLower-income renters, veterans, farmworkers, studentsState General Fund, ~25 years
37Low-down-payment loans for new homesMiddle-income buyers (up to 2× area median income)Borrowers, through bond investors
45Faster, narrower environmental review and lawsuitsBuilders of housing and other covered projectsHigher agency costs at first, partly fee-covered

Prop 37 helps buyers of new homes specifically; how many new homes get built is affected by permitting and review timelines, which is what Prop 45 addresses. The LAO says whether either measure increases total construction is uncertain.

elections.summary: Three independent changes to election rules. No legal conflicts between them.

special.title: Special taxes, state and local
special.summary: Both measures deal with [[special-tax|special taxes]], taxes earmarked for a specific purpose, at different levels of government.
special.body:
• Prop 41 applies to state special taxes: audits before an initiative reaches the ballot and every four years after it passes.
  • Prop 43 applies to local special taxes: citizen-proposed ones would need two-thirds approval instead of a simple majority, starting 2027.

Neither changes taxes already in place. Both make it harder or slower to add new earmarked taxes. Prop 43 is the measure most likely to affect future Santa Clara County and San José ballots.

transit.title: Local taxes and Prop 43
transit.summary: Prop 43 changes the vote needed for citizen-proposed local special taxes, which is exactly how RTM reached the ballot.
transit.body:
• RTM qualified by voter petition, so under current court rulings it passes with a simple majority.
  • Prop 43 would require two-thirds for citizen-proposed local special taxes, but only for new, increased, or extended taxes starting January 1, 2027. It would not apply to RTM on this ballot.
  • If Prop 43 passes, a future renewal of RTM after 14 years, or a similar citizen-led transit or housing tax, would need two-thirds.
  • News reports describe Prop 43 as replacing a broader Howard Jarvis initiative that San José officials warned could have voided Measure E, the city's 2020 property transfer tax for housing and homelessness (about $55M a year). Prop 43 as written applies only going forward, so existing taxes such as Measure E are not affected.

schools.summary: Whether you see these depends on which elementary school district your address is in.

Parcel taxes can pay for teachers and programs. Bonds can only pay for buildings and equipment. Parcel taxes need two-thirds; school bonds need 55% (Prop 39 of 2000).

health.title: Health care funding
health.summary: Three measures that direct or regulate health-related money in different ways.
health.body:
• Prop 40: 90% of a one-time wealth tax goes to health care services. Sponsored by SEIU-UHW.
  • Prop 44: requires nonprofit community clinics to spend 90% of revenue on program services. Also sponsored by SEIU-UHW. Opposed by major physician groups and the clinics.
  • Prop 38: $8.4B in borrowing for immunology research.

Note that the California Primary Care Association, which represents community clinics, is a listed opponent of both Prop 40 and Prop 44.
